title: Project O'Neil
summary: A hybrid 4X and life-simulation game set in the near future of human space habitation — O'Neill cylinders and orbital settlements — built on a framework-agnostic simulation core with two independent frontend MVPs.

en: Project O'Neil is a hybrid 4X and life-simulation game set in the near future of human space habitation. It asks what daily life looks like inside an O'Neill cylinder — and lets the player move between running a settlement and inhabiting a single life within it.

The design holds two scales at once: a macro layer of organizations, star systems and orbital geometry, and a micro layer of individual characters. Both draw from one consistent world state, so a change at either scale stays causally traceable through the simulation rather than scripted.

pull_quote.en: Every visible game state must be causally traceable to simulation inputs — never injected as scripted content.

label.en: Independent frontend MVPs built on one shared simulation

body.en: The simulation is built as a framework-agnostic core, then validated by building two independent frontend MVPs against it. The 3D client uses React Three Fiber to render the star system and habitats as a declarative scene graph — orbital bodies, post-processing effects and selection overlays expressed as React components — with a separate React GUI layer composited on top of the canvas. The second MVP renders the same simulation as a text-based interface with no UI framework at all. Both consume the simulation identically; if either could not, the core was not genuinely decoupled.

steps.en: Model the world as a single shared state spanning macro (organizations, star system) and micro (individual characters) layers.
Drive it with a tick-based simulation covering orbital motion, social, political, and economic systems.
Generate and retire characters on demand within a fixed budget rather than simulating an entire population.

Build a 3D client with React Three Fiber — the star system, orbital bodies and habitats render as a composable scene graph, with Drei helpers and a post-processing pipeline for visual effects, and selection and state overlays expressed as components. It runs as its own React root on a transparent canvas, with an independent React GUI layer composited above for panels and controls.
Build a second, framework-free text UI against the same core to prove it stays framework-agnostic.

title: Neuroglancer (Seung Lab fork)
summary: Seung Lab fork of Google's Neuroglancer — a WebGL volumetric viewer extended with proofreading tools for the FlyWire (fly) and MICrONS (mouse) connectome platforms. Used by 10,000+ proofreaders worldwide; co-credited in three Nature-family papers.

summary.en: Hired in 2019 specifically to extend Neuroglancer for the Seung Lab. Shipped bug-reporting, segment highlighting, state-sharing, and extended annotation tooling that lifted average proofreading turnaround by ~40%. Named co-author on three Nature-family papers.

items.en: Extended Neuroglancer's annotation system with additional tools that improved analyst workflow and lifted average proofreading turnaround ~40%.
Built segment highlighting in the WebGL render path so proofreaders could track a single neuron through dense volumes.
Added in-product bug reporting so the 10,000+ FlyWire proofreader community could flag issues without drowning support.
Implemented state-sharing affordances (viewer pose, layers, selected segments) for collaboration across the proofreader community.
Built the ng-extend Vue wrapper layering chat, tutorials, and community chrome around the embedded Neuroglancer canvas.
Shipped ProofreadingProgress, a Vue + Flask service on Google Cloud that aggregates per-neuron changelogs for publication attribution; cut query response time ~10%.

title: YouTube Tabs Manager
summary: Chrome MV3 side-panel extension that tracks open YouTube tabs, reports live playback analytics, and manages a library of watched videos with sort/filter, tags, and Google Drive sync.

en: A Chrome MV3 side-panel extension for people who keep too many YouTube tabs open. It tracks every open YouTube tab, scrapes best-effort metadata, and listens to the HTML5 video element to report live playback progress — building toward one goal: at most one playback tab open at a time.

The architecture treats the background service worker as the single source of truth. It owns an in-memory store of tabs and videos, persists the library across worker restarts, and broadcasts read-only snapshots to the side panel ~every 750ms. Content scripts run in two worlds — a MAIN-world bridge reads YouTube's internal ytInitialPlayerResponse, while an ISOLATED-world script hooks the video element and relays progress.

Two cross-cutting features layer on top. Playlist-based auto-tagging registers playlists (manually, via OAuth-discovered owned playlists, or by scraping on navigation including Watch Later) and contributes each playlist's name as a dynamically-computed tag. Cross-browser sync round-trips the library, analytics, tags, and playlists through Google Drive's hidden appDataFolder, so multiple browsers signed into the same Google account share one logical library.

pull_quote.en: One playback tab, one library — synced across every browser you sign into.

body.en: State flows in one direction — content script to service worker to side panel — which keeps the UI a pure read-only replica and avoids race conditions across Chrome's process boundaries. Sync uses a hybrid transport: tiny values ride Chrome's native storage.sync, heavy data goes through Drive, and per-device state stays local. Deletions propagate via per-id tombstones with a 30-day TTL so a removal on one browser doesn't get resurrected by a stale copy on another.

steps.en: MAIN-world bridge reads YouTube's internal player data and posts metadata to the ISOLATED content script.
ISOLATED script tracks the video element and forwards progress to the service worker.
Service worker maintains the canonical store, persists the library, and broadcasts snapshots.
Side panel renders each snapshot as a read-only replica with sort, filter, and tagging.
Sync manager pushes structural changes to Google Drive and merges remote state on a 5-minute tick.

title: Twine Deck
summary: A desktop launcher and enhancement shell for Twine interactive fiction — wraps the self-contained HTML files Twine produces inside an Electron app that adds a managed library, a modern save system, variable inspection, and optional mod injection.

en: Twine produces self-contained HTML files for interactive fiction, but offers nothing around them — no managed library, no save handling beyond the story format's own, no way to inspect or edit a running story's state. Twine Deck is a desktop shell that wraps those HTML files inside an Electron application, adding a managed library, a modern save system, variable inspection, and optional mod injection, all without changing how the story itself runs.

The desktop app gives each story a managed library with cover art, tags, and playtime tracking; unlimited named profiles and saves with no slot numbers; a draggable in-game panel for save, load, and profile switching; a live typed editor for the running story's variables; reusable cheat presets; and scoped mod and userscript injection. A companion Node and MongoDB server is planned for a community catalog, accounts, and folder-based sync.

pull_quote.en: The codebase is written to be read.

body.en: Electron splits JavaScript into three contexts — a main process that owns the SQLite database and filesystem, renderer processes that run the React UI, and preload scripts that form a narrow bridge between them. All persistence flows through the main process over typed IPC channels; the renderer never touches the database directly.

steps.en: Each Twine story runs inside its own WebContentsView — a sandboxed browser tab — with a dedicated preload script injected beforehand.
The preload hooks into the story format's save API and exposes a narrow, validated bridge back to the main process; the story cannot call anything the bridge does not explicitly expose.
The floating control panel for saves, profiles, and variables lives in the main window's renderer above the story view, so the story's own code cannot hide or interfere with it.

title: Bomberman AI
summary: ML platform for training agents to play games. Started as an ML project with a custom Bomberman-style game as its training environment, then pivoted into a general platform that trains agents on emulated N64 games behind one unified GameEnvironment interface.

en: Bomberman AI started as a machine-learning project. The Bomberman 64-inspired 3D game was built alongside it as the training environment — a custom, deterministic, tick-authoritative simulation where every state change flows through a discrete 8-step pipeline, making any game state fully reproducible and replayable for an agent to learn from.

The project then pivoted from a single-game ML experiment into the Emulator ML Platform — a more general, TypeScript-first platform for training agents on emulated N64 games. The custom Bomberman engine became one environment among emulator-backed targets like N64Wasm.

Every backend implements one unified GameEnvironment interface. Agents, experiment sessions, and the platform UI interact only through that interface — never with engine or emulator internals — so training code is written once and runs against any game.

pull_quote.en: A single GameEnvironment interface lets one agent train across a custom engine and emulated N64 games.

label.en: Elevation levels in the surface-based 3D world

body.en: The architecture enforces strict separation of concerns. All simulation runs in Web Workers — even the active visible game — so the renderer stays at 60fps and one code path serves live play, headless evaluation, and replay. The React GUI and React Three Fiber renderer consume derived read models, never authoritative state.

steps.en: Run all simulation in workers behind a tick-authoritative pipeline; the main thread is presentation-only.
Route every actor action through an intent system shared by players, bots, and ML models.
Wrap each game backend behind the unified GameEnvironment interface.
Host environments server-side and connect training clients over WebSocket via RemoteGameEnvironment.

title: PolyOCR
summary: Multilingual OCR, machine translation, image inpainting, and region matching — shipped as a headless npm package plus a thin Electron desktop UI that consumes it.

en: PolyOCR is a multilingual OCR pipeline that reads text from images, detects its language, translates it, and — for use cases like manga — inpaints the original text and renders the translation back in place.

It ships as two artifacts that share one pipeline — a headless npm package that does all the real work, and a thin Electron desktop app that is purely a UI consumer of it. The package runs unchanged in a browser extension, a Node CLI, a CI image pipeline, or a server-side render service.

pull_quote.en: Everything that does real work lives in the headless package; the desktop app is just a UI consumer of it.

label.en: Languages translated via the default Ollama backend
Pluggable OCR engines — Tesseract.js and PaddleOCR

body.en: Every pluggable subsystem sits behind a formal TypeScript interface — OcrAdapter, TranslationAdapter, RegionDetector — so a hosted OCR service, a different translation backend, or a custom region matcher can be swapped in without forking the package. The two-process Electron split keeps the OCR pipeline out of the main-process lifecycle, leaving it testable and embeddable.

steps.en: Detect text regions with OpenCV.js contour analysis, with an Ollama vision LLM fallback.
OCR each region with Tesseract.js by default, or PaddleOCR for CJK and complex layouts.
Detect the source language with the franc statistical detector, falling back to an Ollama vision LLM for short or mixed text.
Translate via Ollama by default, or optional DeepL and LibreTranslate adapters.
Inpaint the original text and render the translation back into place.
